title: 一般學術與研究方法論

words.engDef: a whole formed by combining several separate elements; total
words.example: The website calculated the aggregate scores of several independent product reviews.

words.engDef: to make a problem, pain, or suffering less severe or more bearable
words.example: The new drug was designed to alleviate joint stiffness and chronic inflammation.

words.engDef: showing disinterested and selfless concern for the well-being of others
words.example: Many animals display altruistic behaviors, risking their lives to warn the group of predators.

words.engDef: belonging or appropriate to a period other than that in which it exists
words.example: Using paper maps in the age of global positioning systems seems slightly anachronistic.

words.engDef: comparable in certain respects, typically in a way which makes clearer the nature of things
words.example: The wings of a bird are analogous to the wings of an airplane in aerodynamic function.

words.engDef: something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected
words.example: A sudden drop in temperature in July is a weather anomaly for this region.

words.engDef: based on random choice, personal whim, or coincidence, rather than system
words.example: The decision to set the temperature threshold at twenty degrees was entirely arbitrary.

words.engDef: well meaning, kindly, and motivated by a desire to do good
words.example: The museum was built through a massive donation from a benevolent anonymous donor.

words.engDef: a harsh, discordant, and unpleasant mixture of physical sounds
words.example: The market was filled with a loud, chaotic cacophony of vendors shouting and traffic honking.

words.chinese: 變化莫測的，反覆無常的
words.engDef: given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood, behavior, or temperature
words.example: Polar regions are notorious for their capricious weather, shifting from sunshine to blizzards in minutes.

words.chinese: 催化劑，起催化作用的人或物
words.engDef: a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself changing
words.example: Enzymes act as biological catalysts, accelerating vital metabolic processes in our bodies.

words.engDef: kept secret or done secretively, especially because it is illicit
words.example: The rebels held a series of clandestine meetings to organize the defense strategy.

words.engDef: to come together to form one mass, whole, or single system
words.example: The small dust particles began to coalesce under gravity to form early planetary cores.

words.engDef: having knowledge or being fully aware of something
words.example: Astronomers are fully cognizant of the immense scale and dangers of cosmic radiation.

words.engDef: exhibiting or producing physical or logical cohesion; tightly united
words.example: An effective academic paper must present a cohesive and well-structured argument.

words.engDef: to accept, allow, or overlook behavior considered morally wrong or offensive
words.example: The university does not condone plagiarism or academic dishonesty of any kind.

words.engDef: making a certain situation, development, or outcome likely or possible
words.example: A quiet and bright room is highly conducive to deep academic study.

words.engDef: a confusing and highly difficult problem, question, or riddle
words.example: How migrating birds navigate across continents remains a major biological conundrum.

words.engDef: to confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding with evidence
words.example: The defense lawyer presented video footage to corroborate her client’s alibi.

words.engDef: humble submission and respect shown toward elders or specialists
words.example: The young researcher spoke with deep deference in front of the Nobel laureate.

words.engDef: to describe, portray, or outline something precisely
words.example: The topographic map was designed to delineate the exact boundaries of the reserve.

words.engDef: intended to teach, particularly in having moral instruction as a goal
words.example: Fables are famous for their didactic nature, using animal stories to teach moral lessons.

words.chinese: 截然不同的，無從比較的
words.engDef: essentially different in kind; not allowing logical comparison
words.example: The research team combined insights from two highly disparate fields: biology and computer science.

words.engDef: inclined to lay down principles as incontrovertibly true without evidence
words.example: Science thrives on open scrutiny rather than rigid, dogmatic beliefs.

words.engDef: deriving ideas, style, or taste from a broad and diverse range of sources
words.example: The museum's eclectic collection includes tribal masks, modern sculptures, and ancient coins.

words.engDef: outstandingly bad; shocking and flagrant in error
words.rootPrefix: ex- (out) + grex (flock) -> standing out from the flock in a bad way
words.example: The financial report contained several egregious errors that ruined the firm's credibility.

words.engDef: based on, concerned with, or verifiable by observation or experiment rather than theory
words.example: The researcher collected empirical data through a series of lab experiments.

words.engDef: lasting for a very short time; fleeting or transient
words.example: The cherry blossoms of spring are beautiful but highly ephemeral, lasting only a week.

words.engDef: open to more than one interpretation; ambiguous or uncertain
words.example: The results of the laboratory test were highly equivocal, requiring further investigation.

words.engDef: intended for or likely to be understood by only a small group of specialists
words.example: He spent years studying the esoteric grammar rules of ancient Sanskrit texts.

books.title: 一般學術與研究方法論 1

words.engDef: to make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse
words.example: Pumping more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere will exacerbate global warming.

words.engDef: spoken or done without preparation; impromptu
words.example: She was praised for her brilliant, extemporaneous speech during the awards ceremony.

words.engDef: very attentive to and concerned about accuracy, detail, and cleanliness
words.example: The laboratory technician was fastidious, ensuring all glass beakers were sterile.

words.engDef: happening by accident or lucky chance rather than design
words.example: The discovery of penicillin was entirely fortuitous, occurring after a mold contamination.

words.engDef: fond of company; sociable; or living in flocks or herds
words.example: Wolves are highly gregarious mammals that live, travel, and hunt in structured packs.

words.engDef: lacking significance through having been overused; unoriginal
words.rootPrefix: hackney (riding horse for hire) -> hackneyed (common/worn out)
words.example: The movie script was filled with hackneyed plot lines and predictable dialog.

words.chinese: 無計畫的，混亂的，隨意的
words.engDef: lacking any obvious principle of organization, order, or planning
words.example: The books were stacked in a haphazard pile on his crowded study table.

words.engDef: a mode of behavior or way of thought peculiar to an individual
words.example: The author’s primary idiosyncrasy was writing all his novels using a green pen.

words.engDef: unchanging over time or unable to be changed; constant
words.example: The laws of physics are considered immutable truths governing our universe.

words.engDef: acting or done quickly and without thought or care; hasty
words.example: His impetuous decision to quit his academic job surprised all his colleagues.

words.chinese: 似非而是的，不合情理的
words.engDef: not seeming reasonable or probable; highly unlikely to convince
words.example: His excuse for missing the final exam seemed highly implausible to the professor.

words.engDef: not in harmony or keeping with the surroundings or other aspects
words.example: A ultra-modern glass skyscraper looks highly incongruous in the historic old town.

words.chinese: 不知疲倦的，不屈不撓的
words.engDef: persisting tirelessly without showing signs of exhaustion
words.example: The research team’s indefatigable efforts finally led to the medical breakthrough.

words.engDef: lacking the ability or strength to move, or chemically inactive
words.example: Helium and neon are inert gases that do not react easily with other elements.

words.engDef: innocent, unsuspecting, and completely free from deceit
words.example: Her ingenuous nature made it easy for her to trust complete strangers.

words.engDef: tending to obstruct or harm; highly unfriendly or hostile
words.example: High interest rates are highly inimical to small business growth.

words.engDef: lacking flavor, vigor, or interest; weak and tasteless
words.example: The critic dismissed the gallery's new modern exhibition as insipid and boring.

words.engDef: fearless, adventurous, and displaying extreme courage
words.example: The intrepid explorer set off alone to cross the frozen Arctic ice cap.

words.engDef: to overwhelm someone with a huge volume of things or water; flood
words.example: Following the product launch, the support team was inundated with inquiries.

words.engDef: using very few words in speech or writing; concise
words.example: The silent cowboy was famous for his laconic, one-word answers.

words.engDef: expressed clearly; easy to understand; logically structured
words.example: The professor gave a highly lucid explanation of the theory of relativity.

words.engDef: generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or less powerful person
words.example: The victorious general was magnanimous, offering medical aid to defeated troops.

words.engDef: able to be hammered, pressed, or influenced out of shape
words.example: Gold is an extremely malleable metal that can be beaten into thin sheets.

words.engDef: an unorthodox or highly independent-minded person
words.rootPrefix: Samuel Maverick (Texan who did not brand his cattle)
words.example: The young scientist is a maverick who rejects conventional laboratory methods.

words.engDef: a structured system of methods, rules, and principles used in a field of study
words.example: The author included a chapter explaining the research methodology of the survey.

words.engDef: showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise
words.example: The archaeological team made a meticulous record of every shard of pottery discovered.

words.engDef: sullen, gloomy, silent, and ill-tempered in disposition
words.rootPrefix: mos (manner/habit) -> morose (addicted to one's own habits/gloomy)
words.example: The injured dog sat in a corner of the shelter, looking sad and morose.

words.engDef: wicked, criminal, or highly immoral in actions or plans
words.example: The hacker group orchestrated a nefarious plot to steal confidential customer data.

words.engDef: to render obscure, unclear, or highly unintelligible
words.example: The lawyer tried to obfuscate the facts of the case to confuse the jury.

words.engDef: obedient or attentive to an excessive, servile, or fawning degree
words.example: The waiter’s obsequious behavior irritated the diners who preferred quiet service.

books.title: 一般學術與研究方法論 2

words.engDef: to remove a need, difficulty, or potential obstacle
words.example: Installing a new security system will obviate the need for overnight guards.

words.engDef: giving the worrying impression that something bad is going to happen
words.example: Thick black storm clouds gathered in the sky, looking highly ominous.

words.engDef: characterized by vulgar, pretentious, or showy display designed to impress
words.example: The billionaire lived in a massive, ostentatious castle filled with gold statues.

words.engDef: relieving pain or alleviating a problem without curing the underlying cause
words.example: The therapy offers palliative relief to ease the chronic discomfort of patients.

words.engDef: a hypothetical solution or remedy for all diseases, problems, or difficulties
words.example: Technology is a useful tool, but it is not a panacea for all societal problems.

words.engDef: a typical example, pattern, or conceptual model of something
words.example: The Copernican revolution represented a major paradigm shift in astronomy.

words.engDef: excessively concerned with minor academic details, rules, and book learning
words.example: The editor’s corrections were overly pedantic, focusing on tiny punctuation rules.

words.engDef: expressing contempt, disapproval, or a negative judgment
words.example: The critic used several pejorative terms to describe the actor's performance.

words.engDef: a strong or habitual liking for something; a natural inclination
words.example: She has a lifelong penchant for reading science fiction novels during flights.

words.engDef: carried out with a minimum of effort, care, or genuine reflection
words.example: The security guard gave a perfunctory glance at my ID badge before letting me in.

words.engDef: spreading widely throughout an entire physical area, group, or society
words.example: The sweet, rich aroma of baking bread was pervasive throughout the house.

words.chinese: 冷靜的，冷淡的，黏液質的
words.engDef: having an unemotional, stolidly calm, and self-controlled disposition
words.example: Despite the sudden technical crisis, the captain remained completely phlegmatic.

words.engDef: concise, forceful, and extremely expressive in speech or writing
words.example: The writer is famous for her pithy comments that quickly summarize complex issues.

words.engDef: to make someone less angry, hostile, or defensive; soothe
words.example: The hotel offered a complimentary dinner to placate the angry guests.

words.engDef: a large, excessive, or redundant amount of something
words.example: The local library offers a plethora of books on ancient Egyptian history.

words.engDef: a strong, aggressive verbal or written attack on someone or something
words.example: The academic wrote a fierce polemic attacking the university’s new funding policy.

words.engDef: dealing with things realistically based on practical rather than theoretical matters
words.example: The engineers adopted a pragmatic approach to fix the bridge quickly.

words.engDef: not securely held in position; dangerously likely to fall, fail, or collapse
words.rootPrefix: precarius (obtained by entreaty/prayer -> dependent on another's will -> unstable)
words.example: The small wooden cabin was built in a precarious position on the edge of the steep cliff.

words.engDef: dangerously high, steep, or showing a rapid, sudden drop
words.example: Farms suffered heavy losses due to a precipitous drop in potato market prices.

words.engDef: to prevent from happening; make a development completely impossible
words.example: Failing to obtain a visa will preclude you from traveling to the conference.

words.engDef: a person or thing that comes before another of the same kind; forerunner
words.example: The discovery of simple cave drawings was a precursor to the development of written languages.

words.engDef: a strong preference or special liking for something; partiality
words.example: He has an outstanding predilection for classical music, spending hours listening to Beethoven.

words.engDef: a natural tendency to choose or do something regularly; inclination
words.example: The hyperactive puppy has a strong proclivity for chewing on leather shoes.

words.engDef: remarkably or impressively great in extent, size, degree, or force
words.example: The young pianist displayed prodigious talent, performing complex sonatas at age six.

words.engDef: an natural inclination or natural tendency to behave in a particular way
words.example: She has a lifelong propensity to exaggerate her adventures to surprise her friends.

words.engDef: eager or quick to argue, quarrel, or fight; aggressively defiant
words.example: The bar owner had to eject several pugnacious customers to maintain order.

words.engDef: showing great attention to detail, correct behavior, and strict etiquette
words.example: The diplomatic secretary was punctilious, ensuring all guests were seated in exact order.

words.engDef: relating to, measuring, or measured by the quality of something rather than numbers
words.example: The sociologist conducted qualitative interviews to gather detailed personal stories.

words.engDef: a state of perplexity or uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
words.example: He was in a quandary about whether to accept the job offer or continue his PhD studies.

words.engDef: relating to, measuring, or measured by the quantity or numerical values
words.example: The study utilized quantitative analysis to calculate exact statistical correlation.

books.title: 一般學術與研究方法論 3

words.engDef: in a state or period of temporary inactivity, stillness, or dormancy
words.example: The volcano has been quiescent for over a century, but scientists monitor it closely.

words.engDef: long-standing, deep bitterness or resentfulness
words.example: The legal dispute was settled without any remaining rancor between the former partners.

words.engDef: having an obstinately uncooperative attitude toward authority or rules
words.example: The school has a special program to counsel recalcitrant students and rebuild their trust.

words.engDef: of a subject or knowledge little known; abstruse or highly esoteric
words.example: The professor spent decades researching recondite areas of medieval philosophy.

words.engDef: to dismiss or banish to an inferior rank, role, or position
words.example: The veteran player was disappointed to find himself relegated to the substitute bench.

words.engDef: deserving of severe censure, condemnation, or blame
words.example: Animal abuse is a highly reprehensible act that carries heavy legal penalties.

words.engDef: to refuse to accept, be associated with, or recognize the validity of
words.example: The senator issued a statement to repudiate the false claims made by the opposition.

words.engDef: to revoke, cancel, or repeal a law, agreement, or official order
words.example: The city council voted to rescind the controversial tax hike after public protests.

words.engDef: not revealing one's thoughts, feelings, or plans readily; reserved
words.example: He is highly reticent about his private life, rarely sharing details during interviews.

words.engDef: most noticeable, prominent, or important; outstanding
words.example: The summary highlights the salient points of the lengthy environmental report.

words.engDef: producing highly beneficial and good effects; health-giving
words.example: The brief crisis served as a salutary lesson, forcing us to tighten our data security.

words.chinese: 道貌岸然的，假裝虔誠的
words.engDef: making a hypocritical show of being morally superior or pious
words.example: The corrupt politician’s sanctimonious speech about honesty disgusted the public.

words.chinese: 謹慎的，恪守道德的，一絲不苟的
words.engDef: diligent, thorough, and extremely attentive to details; morally upright
words.example: The accountant maintained highly scrupulous financial records for the non-profit group.

words.chinese: 機緣巧合，善於發現新奇事物的能力
words.engDef: the occurrence of beneficial events by happy chance or coincidence
words.rootPrefix: Serendip (Persian name for Sri Lanka) -> tale of Three Princes of Serendip
words.example: The discovery of the ancient tomb was a stroke of pure, beautiful serendipity.

words.chinese: 似是而非的，華而不實的
words.engDef: superficially plausible, but actually wrong or misleading
words.example: The politician presented a specious argument that was easily refuted by experts.

words.engDef: not being what it purports to be; false, fake, or illegitimate
words.example: The antiques expert easily identified the signed document as a spurious fake.

words.engDef: to provide concrete evidence to support or prove the truth of a claim
words.example: You need to present physical evidence to substantiate your charges in court.

words.engDef: seeking or intending to subvert or ruin an established system
words.example: The organization was banned for distributing highly subversive pamphlets.

words.engDef: briefly, clearly, and logically expressed; concise
words.example: The executive brief provides a succinct summary of the corporate strategy.

words.engDef: unnecessary, especially through being more than enough; redundant
words.example: Please delete any superfluous details to make the research summary concise.

words.engDef: kept secret, especially because it would not be officially approved of
words.example: She took a surreptitious glance at her phone during the boring lecture.

words.engDef: a person who acts obsequiously toward powerful figures to gain advantage
words.example: The tyrant was surrounded by sycophants who praised his every foolish decision.

words.engDef: understood or implied without being explicitly stated in words
words.example: There was a tacit agreement among the flatmates regarding the cleaning roster.

words.engDef: reserved, silent, or highly uncommunicative in speech
words.example: His grandfather was a quiet, taciturn man who rarely shared his thoughts.

words.engDef: tending to keep a extremely firm hold of something; clinging closely
words.example: Ivy is a highly tenacious climbing plant that clings tightly to old stone walls.

words.engDef: very weak, slight, or insubstantial; highly fragile
words.example: The link between the two events is tenuous, lacking concrete evidence.

words.engDef: a long, angry, and highly critical speech of accusation
words.example: The coach launched into a loud tirade against the team's poor performance.

words.chinese: 遲鈍的，蟄伏的，不活潑的
words.engDef: mentally or physically inactive; highly lethargic and slow
words.example: Hibernating mammals remain in a torpid state during freezing winter months.

words.engDef: easy to control, influence, guide, or manage
words.example: The young horse was highly tractable, learning to follow instructions quickly.

words.engDef: lasting only for a very short time; temporary or impermanent
words.example: The glowing colors of the sunset were beautiful but highly transient.

books.title: 一般學術與研究方法論 4

words.engDef: a feeling of fear, agitation, or deep anxiety about something that may happen
words.example: She approached the interview room with a sense of nervous trepidation.

words.engDef: eager or quick to argue or fight; aggressively defiant and hostile
words.example: The prisoner became truculent, refusing to cooperate with the guards.

words.chinese: 無所不在的，普遍存在的
words.engDef: present, appearing, or found everywhere at the same time
words.example: Microscopic dust mites are ubiquitous in almost all household environments.

words.chinese: 站不住腳的，難以防守的
words.engDef: not able to be maintained or defended against logical objection
words.example: The scientist's theory became untenable after the new data disproved it.

words.engDef: to waver between different opinions or actions; be highly indecisive
words.example: She continued to vacillate between choosing biology or chemistry as her major.

words.engDef: to regard with great respect; revere and honor
words.example: The local tribes venerate the giant oak tree as a sacred symbol of nature.

words.engDef: conformity to facts; absolute accuracy and truthfulness
words.example: The jury questioned the veracity of the witness's confusing statements.

words.engDef: using or expressed in more words than are logically needed
words.example: The editor trimmed the verbose paragraph to make the article succinct.

words.engDef: to clear someone of blame or suspicion with concrete evidence
words.example: The newly discovered laboratory notes helped to vindicate the accused scientist.

words.chinese: 劇毒的，致命的，有惡意的
words.engDef: of a disease or poison extremely severe, harmful, or deadly
words.example: The hospital is treating patients infected with a highly virulent strain of flu.

words.engDef: wanting or devouring great quantities of food; extremely eager
words.example: The active child is a voracious reader, finishing three books every week.
